title: What are ConcurrentSkipListMap and ConcurrentSkipListSet, how does a skip list give O(log n) sorted access concurrently, and when do you choose them over ConcurrentHashMap?

s1_definition.profdef: `ConcurrentSkipListMap` is a thread-safe, sorted map backed by a skip list, giving O(log n) `get`, `put`, and `remove` while keeping keys in sorted order and supporting the full `NavigableMap` API (`firstKey`, `ceilingKey`, `headMap`, `subMap`). `ConcurrentSkipListSet` is the set built on the same structure. A skip list is a layered linked list: the bottom layer holds all elements in order, and higher layers are express lanes that let a search skip over many nodes, achieving logarithmic time. It uses lock-free CAS operations, so it scales without global locking. You choose it over `ConcurrentHashMap` when you need the keys kept sorted or need range and nearest-key queries; ConcurrentHashMap is faster (O(1)) but unordered.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps all trade orders pinned on a very long board in price order. `ConcurrentHashMap` is like a cloakroom with numbered hooks: you find any one ticket instantly, but the tickets are in no particular order, so you cannot ask "give me all tickets priced between 2400 and 2500." A skip list is like that price-ordered board with extra shortcut rails above it: a top rail lets a clerk jump every hundredth order, a middle rail every tenth, and the bottom rail is every order. To find a price the clerk rides the express rails down, skipping huge chunks, and lands near the target in a few hops. Because the board is always sorted, range questions and nearest-price questions are easy, and multiple clerks can work on different sections at once without one big lock.
s1_definition.oneliner: ConcurrentSkipListMap is the thread-safe sorted map — O(log n) with ordered keys and range queries via a lock-free skip list; use it over ConcurrentHashMap only when you actually need sorting or navigation.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `ConcurrentSkipListMap` is a thread-safe, sorted map backed by a skip list, giving O(log n) `get`, `put`, and `remove` while keeping keys in sorted order and supporting the full `NavigableMap` API (`firstKey`, `ceilingKey`, `headMap`, `subMap`). `ConcurrentSkipListSet` is the set built on the same structure. A skip list is a layered linked list: the bottom layer holds all elements in order, and higher layers are express lanes that let a search skip over many nodes, achieving logarithmic time. It uses lock-free CAS operations, so it scales without global locking. You choose it over `ConcurrentHashMap` when you need the keys kept sorted or need range and nearest-key queries; ConcurrentHashMap is faster (O(1)) but unordered.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps all trade orders pinned on a very long board in price order. `ConcurrentHashMap` is like a cloakroom with numbered hooks: you find any one ticket instantly, but the tickets are in no particular order, so you cannot ask "give me all tickets priced between 2400 and 2500." A skip list is like that price-ordered board with extra shortcut rails above it: a top rail lets a clerk jump every hundredth order, a middle rail every tenth, and the bottom rail is every order. To find a price the clerk rides the express rails down, skipping huge chunks, and lands near the target in a few hops. Because the board is always sorted, range questions and nearest-price questions are easy, and multiple clerks can work on different sections at once without one big lock.

**One line to remember:** ConcurrentSkipListMap is the thread-safe sorted map — O(log n) with ordered keys and range queries via a lock-free skip list; use it over ConcurrentHashMap only when you actually need sorting or navigation.

sections.s2_technical:
You create one with `ConcurrentSkipListMap<K,V> book = new ConcurrentSkipListMap<>()` and it keeps keys in natural order, or you pass a `Comparator` for custom order such as descending price. Basic `put`, `get`, and `remove` work like any map but run in O(log n) because of the skip-list search.

The navigation methods are the reason to pick it. `firstKey()` and `lastKey()` give the smallest and largest keys, useful for the best bid and best ask in an order book: `book.firstKey()` returns the lowest price instantly. `ceilingKey(k)` returns the smallest key greater than or equal to k, so `book.ceilingEntry(new BigDecimal("2450"))` finds the first order at or above 2450. `floorKey`, `higherKey`, and `lowerKey` are the related variants. `subMap(from, to)`, `headMap(to)`, and `tailMap(from)` return live sorted views over a range, which is exactly how you pull "all orders between 2400 and 2500."

```java
ConcurrentSkipListMap<BigDecimal, Order> asks = new ConcurrentSkipListMap<>();
asks.put(new BigDecimal("2450.50"), order1);
asks.put(new BigDecimal("2448.00"), order2);
BigDecimal bestAsk = asks.firstKey();                 // lowest price = 2448.00
var band = asks.subMap(new BigDecimal("2400"), new BigDecimal("2500"));  // range view
```

The skip list itself is layered. Every element sits in the bottom list in sorted order. Each element is also promoted to higher express lanes with decreasing probability (roughly one in two for level 2, one in four for level 3, and so on), so the top lanes are sparse. A search starts at the top-left, moves right until the next node would overshoot the target, drops down a level, and repeats, which halves the remaining search each level, giving O(log n).

Concurrency is lock-free: insertions and deletions use compare-and-swap on individual node links rather than a global lock, so many threads read and write concurrently with high throughput, and iterators are weakly consistent, meaning they never throw ConcurrentModificationException and reflect some but not necessarily all concurrent updates.

The senior decision: ConcurrentHashMap gives O(1) and is faster for pure key lookups but has no ordering. ConcurrentSkipListMap gives O(log n) but keeps order and supports navigation. So I reach for the skip list only when the domain genuinely needs sorted iteration, range scans, or nearest-key lookups, such as an order book or a time-ordered event log; otherwise ConcurrentHashMap wins on raw speed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs an equity order-matching engine. Buy and sell orders for a stock like RELIANCE arrive continuously from many threads, and the engine constantly needs the best price: the lowest ask and the highest bid. With an unordered map it would have to scan every order to find the minimum. This is exactly what ConcurrentSkipListMap solves: keyed by price, the lowest ask is just `firstKey()` and the highest bid is `lastKey()`, both in logarithmic time, while many feed threads insert concurrently without a global lock.

Problem 2 — The risk desk wants all resting orders in a price band, say between Rs.2,400 and Rs.2,500, to assess exposure. A sorted map answers this with a single `subMap` range view instead of scanning everything.

Problem 3 — A watchlist of unique traded symbols must stay alphabetically sorted for the UI, and many threads add symbols. ConcurrentSkipListSet keeps the set sorted and thread-safe at once.

The code builds an `Order` record, an `OrderBook` using a ConcurrentSkipListMap keyed by price for asks and bids, methods `addAsk`, `bestAsk`, and `ordersInBand`, a ConcurrentSkipListSet watchlist, and a demo with several threads inserting orders for RELIANCE and querying the best price.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: six ask orders for RELIANCE at prices 2450.50, 2448.00, 2455.75, 2448.00 (duplicate key), 2460.00, 2452.25, inserted concurrently by four threads.

Step 1: Each thread calls `addAsk`, which does `asks.put(price, order)`. The skip list places each price in sorted position using a lock-free CAS on the node links, so concurrent inserts do not block each other. The duplicate 2448.00 overwrites the earlier order at that key (a map keeps one value per key).

Step 2: After all inserts and the completion latch opens, the internal order by price is 2448.00, 2450.50, 2452.25, 2455.75, 2460.00.

Step 3: `bestAsk()` calls `firstKey()`, which rides the express lanes to the leftmost node in O(log n) and returns Rs.2448.00 — the best price a buyer would hit.

Step 4: `ordersInBand(2448, 2453)` calls `subMap`, returning a sorted live view containing the orders at 2448.00, 2450.50, and 2452.25 (the upper bound 2453 is exclusive), so three orders.

Step 5: The watchlist, a ConcurrentSkipListSet, received many `add("RELIANCE")` calls from different threads but keeps only one sorted unique entry. The final output lists the best ask, the banded orders, and the sorted watchlist.

sections.s6_takeaway:
ConcurrentSkipListMap is the thread-safe sorted map in the Java concurrency library, and ConcurrentSkipListSet is the set built on the same structure. It keeps keys in sorted order and gives logarithmic time for get, put, and remove, and it implements the full navigable interface, so I get firstKey, lastKey, ceilingKey, floorKey, and range views like subMap, headMap, and tailMap.

Under the hood it is a skip list, which is a stack of linked lists. The bottom list holds every element in sorted order, and above it are sparse express lanes where each element is promoted with decreasing probability. A search starts at the top-left express lane, moves right until the next hop would overshoot the target, drops down one level, and repeats. Because each level roughly halves the remaining distance, the search is logarithmic. The structure is lock-free: inserts and removes use compare-and-swap on individual node links rather than a global lock, so many threads operate concurrently with high throughput, and its iterators are weakly consistent, so they never throw a concurrent modification exception.

The decision between this and ConcurrentHashMap comes down to one question: do I need ordering? ConcurrentHashMap gives me constant-time lookups and is faster, but it is completely unordered, so it cannot answer "what is the smallest key" or "give me everything in this range" without scanning the whole thing. ConcurrentSkipListMap is a bit slower at logarithmic time, but it keeps everything sorted and answers nearest-key and range queries directly. So I only reach for the skip list when the domain genuinely needs sorted iteration or navigation.

At National Bank of India the perfect fit was the equity order-matching engine. I kept the ask side of the book in a ConcurrentSkipListMap keyed by price, so the best ask was just firstKey in logarithmic time while dozens of feed threads inserted orders concurrently without a global lock. When the risk desk wanted every resting order in a price band, I answered it with a single subMap range view instead of scanning. And I kept the traded-symbol watchlist in a ConcurrentSkipListSet so it stayed alphabetically sorted and thread-safe at the same time. The sentence I give interviewers is that ConcurrentSkipListMap is the sorted, navigable, lock-free concurrent map — I choose it over ConcurrentHashMap only when I actually need the keys ordered or need range and nearest-key queries, and I accept its logarithmic cost in exchange for that ordering.
